text:
Opening Statement This complaint concerns a foreclosure proceeding in which the mortgage servicer relied on a vendor declaration stating that a Notice of Trustee Sale was posted at my property. Documentation from the entity responsible for managing access to the gated community where the property is located confirms that the posting agent never requested entry and never accessed the community. This raises serious concerns regarding the accuracy of the foreclosure vendors declaration and the servicers oversight of foreclosure notice procedures. 



Complaint Summary This complaint concerns defective foreclosure notice procedures and inaccurate vendor declarations used in connection with foreclosure activity involving the property located in XXXX XXXX, XXXX. 

A posting affidavit prepared by a foreclosure vendor states that the Notice of Trustee Sale was posted at the property on XX/XX/XXXX. 

However, documentation from the XXXX XXXX Community Services District, which manages the controlled-access entrance to the community where the property is located, confirms that no process server or posting agent requested entry into the community on that date. 

Because the property is located inside a gated community that requires access authorization to enter, the posting agent could not have reached the property without requesting entry. 

This raises concerns that the declaration stating the notice was posted at the property may be inaccurate. 



Evidence Supporting This Complaint Vendor Posting Declaration A document titled Proof of Notice of Trustee Sale Posting prepared by the foreclosure vendor indicates that the Notice of Trustee Sale was posted on XX/XX/XXXX at the property address. 

The declaration indicates that the notice was posted at locations including the front door, gate, or garage of the property. 



Community Access Records XXXX XXXX XXXX Community Services District reviewed its records and confirmed the following regarding the date of the alleged posting : No process server or posting agent requested entry into the community No authorization for entry was granted No identification of an individual serving foreclosure documents was recorded No administrative record exists showing entry by a posting agent Because the property is located within a controlled-access gated community, entry authorization is required in order to physically reach the property. 

These records indicate that no such entry occurred. 



Documentation of Gate Posting The district further confirmed that on XX/XX/XXXX, an individual approached the community entrance gate and placed papers on the gate without requesting authorization to enter the community. 

The entrance gate serves more than XXXX homes and is located approximately XXXX mile from the property. 

Placing papers on the entrance gate is not equivalent to posting notice at the property itself. 



Material Discrepancy in Foreclosure Documentation The vendor declaration states that the Notice of Trustee Sale was posted at the property address. 

However, the access records maintained by the entity responsible for managing entry into the gated community confirm that the posting agent never requested entry and therefore never reached the property. 

This creates a significant discrepancy between the foreclosure vendors declaration and the independent records documenting access to the community. 



Consumer Protection Concerns Mortgage servicers remain responsible for the conduct of third-party vendors acting on their behalf during foreclosure proceedings. 

When foreclosure activity relies on vendor declarations, the servicer must ensure that those declarations are accurate and supported by verifiable documentation. 

Proceeding with foreclosure activity based on inaccurate vendor declarations raises concerns regarding unfair or deceptive servicing practices and inadequate oversight of foreclosure vendors. 



Requested Investigation I respectfully request that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau investigate whether : 1. The foreclosure vendor submitted an inaccurate declaration regarding the posting of the Notice of Trustee Sale 2. The mortgage servicer relied on vendor documentation that conflicts with independent access records 3. Adequate oversight of foreclosure vendors was conducted 4. The foreclosure process relied on defective statutory notice procedures Requested Resolution I request that the servicer : Explain how the notice could have been posted at the property when the posting agent never accessed the community Produce the documentation supporting the alleged posting of the Notice of Trustee Sale on XX/XX/XXXX, including the vendor work order, service logs, and any photographs taken by the posting vendor showing where the notice was posted Confirm whether foreclosure activity relied on inaccurate vendor declarations Suspend foreclosure activity until this discrepancy is fully investigated Supporting Documentation The following documents support this complaint : Posting affidavit / proof of posting prepared by the foreclosure vendor Written confirmation from the XXXX XXXX Community Services District regarding access records and entry procedures Potential Systemic Concern The discrepancy between the foreclosure vendors declaration and the independent access records maintained by the XXXX XXXX Community Services District raises concerns that inaccurate posting declarations may have been submitted in connection with foreclosure proceedings. 

If a foreclosure vendor is submitting declarations stating that notices were posted at properties when access records show the vendor never entered the community where the property is located, this raises broader concerns regarding the accuracy of foreclosure documentation and the adequacy of servicer oversight of third-party vendors. 

I respectfully request that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau determine whether similar practices may have occurred in other foreclosure proceedings involving this servicer or its vendors. 



Additional Context The documentation from the XXXX XXXX Community Services District dated XX/XX/XXXX has also been submitted as Exhibit C in pending court filings related to this matter. The court has not yet issued its order regarding those filings. 

Because this documentation is already part of the evidentiary record before the court, the discrepancy between the foreclosure vendors declaration and the community access records is currently under review. 

I am providing the same documentation to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau so that the accuracy of the foreclosure notice procedures and the servicers oversight of its foreclosure vendors can also be evaluated. 

Because the documentation referenced in this complaint is already part of pending court filings and directly contradicts the foreclosure vendors declaration regarding the posting of the Notice of Trustee Sale, I respectfully request that Wells Fargo conduct an immediate review of the foreclosure file to ensure that the foreclosure process has relied on accurate documentation and proper statutory notice procedures.

text:
I am filing this complaint against SoFi Bank, N.A. ( " SoFi '' ) in connection with my student loan refinance. I believe SoFi has engaged in deceptive and misleading disclosure practices regarding the application of a XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX discount to my interest rate, and has breached the material representations it made to me prior to and at the time of loan origination. 

I refinanced my student loans with SoFi through the SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX program, which is available to XXXX  of SoFi 's XXXX XXXX  companies. At the time I applied, the SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX website described the XXXX  discount as follows : " XXXX  % rate discount for refinancing your student loan : Terms and conditions apply. Offer good for new student loan refinancing customers only and subject to lender approval. To receive the offer, you must : ( 1 ) register and/or apply through this landing page/your SoFi XXXX XXXX Dashboard or Benefits Portal ; ( 2 ) complete a loan application with SoFi within 90 days of your application submit date ; ( 3 ) and meet SoFi 's underwriting criteria XXXX Once conditions are met and the loan has been disbursed, the interest rate shown in the Final Disclosure Statement will include an additional XXXX  % rate discount because of your involvement with a SoFi XXXX  company at the time of loan origination. '' This language is unambiguous : SoFi represented that the XXXX  % XXXX  discount would be reflected as an additional discount in the Final Disclosure Statement, applied after disbursement of the loan. I satisfied all of the stated conditions for receiving this discount. 

I signed a document entitled " SOFI BANK, N.A. REFI EDUCATION LOAN FIXED RATE APPROVAL DISCLOSURE '' ( the " Disclosure '' ). The Disclosure stated that the initial interest rate without discount would be XXXX  %. The Disclosure further stated that the interest rate " does not reflect qualifying discounts, such as Autopay Discount and SoFi Plus Discount. '' It did not indicate that the corporate partner discount had already been factored into the stated rate, nor did it disclose that the corporate discount was not a " qualifying discount '' for purposes of that disclosure. 

By using the phrase " such as '' when listing qualifying discounts, the Disclosure impliedbut did not excludethe existence of additional qualifying discounts, including the corporate partner discount. I reasonably understood, based on SoFi 's explicit written representations on its SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX website, that the corporate discount would be applied and separately reflected in a Final Disclosure Statement following disbursement. No such Final Disclosure Statement reflecting the additional XXXX  % discount was ever provided. 

Additionally, the Disclosure 's Reference Notes stated : " From time to time, you might be eligible for discounts and/or interest rate deductions offered by SoFi. Please refer to the terms for such offers located on the SoFi website. '' This language directly directed me to SoFi 's website terms the very terms that represented the corporate discount would be applied as an additional post-disbursement reduction. 

Once the loan was dispersed, I called SoFi to ask why my rate shown was XXXX  % and asked when the .XXXX  % corporate discount would be applied. I was then told by customer service that it had already been applied so I decided to press the issue out of confusion. When I escalated the issue with SoFi, a Resolution Specialist responded that : 1. The corporate discount had already been applied during the application process and was embedded in the XXXX  % rate shown in my Disclosure ( i.e., the initial rate before the XXXX discount was allegedly XXXX  % ) ; XXXX. The XXXX  discount is " permanent '' and therefore is not disclosed separately in the loan documents and is given at some point in the application process that I would not have any record of ; 3. The terms I cited were from a source dated XX/XX/year> and that SoFi reserves the right to change or terminate its discount program. 

I find this response inadequate and misleading for the following reasons : I can not find any record of a corporate discount being disclosed. Neither my Disclosure nor any other loan document I received identified the corporate discount, its amount, or the fact that it had been applied. If the corporate discount was embedded in the XXXX  % rate, SoFi was obligated to disclose it as such ( and even if they did disclose it in the application process, there should be some kind of record of this application in the documentation I signed which there was not ). Concealing a discount within a stated rate is not a transparent or adequate disclosure, particularly where SoFi 's own written materials represented it would be separately identified in a Final Disclosure Statement.

SoFi 's terms expressly stated the discount would be applied after disbursement. The plain language of SoFi 's SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX terms states the discount would appear in the Final Disclosure Statement after disbursement not before. SoFi can not now retroactively recharacterize the discount as having been applied during the application stage. This is inconsistent with its own representations. 

The argument that the terms were outdated is unavailing. SoFi did not notify me prior to or at the time of my loan application that the terms on the SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX website were outdated, inapplicable, or had been superseded. I relied in good faith on the representations set out on SoFi 's own platform when deciding to refinance through the SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX program. 

SoFi has failed to respond to my follow-up request. After receiving SoFi 's initial response, I replied requesting that SoFi apply the disputed XXXX  % discount to my ongoing interest rate on both a going-forward and retroactive basis. SoFi did not respond to this request. I have also made multiple phone calls to SoFi 's customer service, and representatives have told me there is nothing they can do to help. 

As a direct result of SoFi 's failure to properly apply the XXXX  % corporate discount as represented : 1. I am paying an interest rate of XXXX % rather than the XXXX  % I am entitled to under SoFi 's own terms.

2. I have been and continue to be overcharged interest on the outstanding principal balance of my loan.

3. I relied on SoFi 's material representations in entering into this loan and would not have done so on the same terms had SoFi 's representations been accurate and complete. 

While XXXX % may appear to be a modest figure in isolation, when applied to a loan balance over the full term of the loan, it represents a meaningful financial harm to me. I also have reason to believe that other SoFi borrowers who refinanced through the SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX program may be in the same situation, having similarly relied on SoFi 's representations without receiving the benefit of the promised discount.
label: Student loan

The law applies to all schools that receive funds under an applicable program of the U.S. Department of Education.

FERPA gives parents certain rights with respect to their children 's education records. These rights transfer to the student when he or she reaches the age of XXXX or attends a school beyond the high school level. Students to whom the rights have transferred are " eligible students. '' Parents or eligible students have the right to inspect and review the student 's education records maintained by the school. Schools are not required to provide copies of records unless, for reasons such as great distance, it is impossible for parents or eligible students to review the records. Schools may charge a fee for copies. 
Parents or eligible students have the right to request that a school correct records which they believe to be inaccurate or misleading. If the school decides not to amend the record, the parent or eligible student then has the right to a formal hearing. After the hearing, if the school still decides not to amend the record, the parent or eligible student has the right to place a statement with the record setting forth his or her view about the contested information. 
Generally, schools must have written permission from the parent or eligible student in order to release any information from a student 's education record. However, FERPA allows schools to disclose those records, without consent, to the following parties or under the following conditions ( 34 CFR 99.31 ) : School officials with legitimate educational interest ; Other schools to which a student is transferring ; Specified officials for audit or evaluation purposes ; Appropriate parties in connection with financial aid to a student ; Organizations conducting certain studies for or on behalf of the school ; Accrediting organizations ; To comply with a judicial order or lawfully issued subpoena ; Appropriate officials in cases of health and safety emergencies ; and State and local authorities, within a juvenile justice system, pursuant to specific State law.

To Whom It May Concern, I am submitting this response regarding Shellpoint Mortgage Servicings XX/XX/XXXX, response to my CFPB complaint concerning my mortgage loan, Trial Period Plan, and loan modification review. 

While I appreciate Shellpoints acknowledgment that service and system issues affected my ability to submit my XX/XX/XXXX trial payment, I respectfully dispute several of the companys conclusions and request an additional review and investigation. 

First, I want to make clear that I have consistently acted in good faith and have always intended to keep my home and continue making affordable mortgage payments. 

Shellpoints response confirms : * Their online payment portal reflected additional fees that prevented submission of the required trial payment amount. 
* I mailed a payment in good faith during the servicing transfer period. 
* The payment was returned after being sent to the prior servicer. 
* I immediately contacted Shellpoint seeking alternative payment options. 
* The final trial payment was ultimately accepted, and * The trial modification was not canceled due to the payment submission issues. 

However, the primary issue remains unresolved. 

When I entered the Trial Period Plan in XX/XX/XXXX, I reasonably believed that successful completion of the trial payments would result in an affordable and sustainable permanent mortgage payment close to my prior payment amount of approximately {$3400.00}. 

I was instructed to make : * an initial payment of {$500.00} ; and * three trial payments of {$7200.00}.

During conversations with Shellpoint representatives, including representative XXXX XXXX, I was never clearly informed that the permanently modified mortgage payment would become approximately {$7100.00} per month. 

The first written documentation clearly stating a permanent payment of {$7100.00} appears in the XX/XX/XXXX, modification package. Prior to that time, Shellpoints Trial Period Plan documents repeatedly described the modification as a path toward more affordable mortgage payments and more manageable terms.

The Trial Period Plan documents also stated : Any difference between the amount of the trial period payments and your regular mortgage payments should not significantly change the amount of your modified mortgage payment.

A permanent payment of {$7100.00} was more than twice my original mortgage payment and was not affordable, manageable, or sustainable given my financial circumstances.

Additionally, Shellpoints own online servicing portal continued to display : * Monthly Payment : {$3400.00} ; and * Starting XX/XX/XXXX, your new payment will be {$3500.00}. 

This directly contradicts the separate modification documents, which state that my payment would be {$7100.00} effective XX/XX/XXXX. 

These conflicting and inconsistent payment disclosures created substantial confusion and reinforced my understanding that my permanent modified payment would remain near my prior affordable payment level. 

I also respectfully dispute the characterization that I voluntarily canceled the loan modification. 

I did not reject mortgage assistance or refuse to keep my home. Rather, after reviewing the proposed permanent terms, I informed Shellpoint that : * The payment was unaffordable. 
* My income had changed due to job loss and reduced earnings. 
* I wanted to provide updated financial documentation. 
* I wanted a new, affordable loan modification review based on my current income, and * I wanted to continue making affordable monthly payments while a review was pending. 

I specifically informed Shellpoint that I had lost my previous job and later secured new employment at a lower income level. 

I attempted to provide updated financial information and supporting documentation reflecting my current financial circumstances. However, Shellpoint representatives informed me that updated financial documents were not needed because they already had all our information on file. 

Further, when I later attempted to pursue a new modification review, I was unable to properly submit a new loan modification application and updated financial documentation because I was effectively prevented or blocked from submitting a new review request. 

I can afford payments approximately equal to my prior monthly mortgage payment of {$3400.00}, but I can not afford a payment over {$7000.00} per month. A modification that more than doubles my monthly payment is neither sustainable, affordable, or realistic given my current income and financial circumstances.

I continue to request : 1. A full reevaluation for an affordable loan modification using my CURRENT income and financial documentation ; 2. Written clarification regarding the conflicting payment amounts reflected in Shellpoints online portal and modification documents ; 3. Copies of all : * call recordings; * servicing notes; * underwriting calculations; * affordability analyses; * investor restrictions; * and internal records regarding my modification review ; 4. Written confirmation that I may continue making affordable monthly payments while the loss mitigation review is pending ; 5. Confirmation that foreclosure activity will remain paused while this dispute and modification review remain unresolved.

I respectfully request that CFPB continue reviewing this matter, including the inconsistent payment disclosures, the affordability determination process, the denial of meaningful reconsideration, and the inability to submit a new modification application using updated financial information.

text:
I am filing this complaint due to the continued reporting of unauthorized hard inquiries on my consumer credit reports and the failure of the credit reporting agencies to properly investigate and remove fraudulent information in violation of the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ). 

I am a confirmed victim of identity theft. I filed an official Identity Theft Report with the Federal Trade Commission ( FTC Report Number : XXXX ), which documents fraudulent and unauthorized inquiries that appeared on my credit reports. A copy of this FTC report has already been provided to the credit reporting agencies. 

The unauthorized inquiries include : XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XX/XX/XXXX XXXX XXXX XX/XX/XXXX XXXX XX/XX/XXXX These inquiries were not authorized by me. I did not apply for credit with these entities, I did not initiate any transaction with them, and I did not provide written, verbal, electronic, or implied consent for them to access my consumer report. 

Under FCRA 604 ( 15 U.S.C. 1681b ), a creditor must have a permissible purpose before accessing a consumer report. No permissible purpose exists here. Accessing my credit file without authorization constitutes unlawful access and a violation of federal law. 

Additionally, under FCRA 605B, once a consumer submits a valid Identity Theft Report, the credit reporting agencies are required to block and remove information resulting from identity theft. I provided an FTC Identity Theft Report clearly identifying these inquiries as fraudulent. Despite this, the inquiries continue to report. 

Under FCRA 611, the credit reporting agencies are required to conduct a reasonable reinvestigation of disputed information. A reasonable reinvestigation requires more than automated verification. I formally requested : The method of verification used The source relied upon A copy of the original signed application Documentation proving permissible purpose Proof of written authorization To date, I have not received competent evidence showing that I authorized these inquiries. 

I have also been impacted by the Equifax XXXX XXXX and the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, significantly increasing the likelihood that my personal identifying information was compromised and used fraudulently. Given this elevated risk, the continued reporting of unauthorized inquiries reflects a failure to apply heightened scrutiny as required when identity theft is documented. 

Furthermore, I have disputed inaccurate personal identifiers appearing on my credit files, including incorrect names, outdated or inaccurate addresses, and incorrect employer information. Reporting inaccurate personal identifiers exposes me to additional identity theft risk and violates the requirement to maintain maximum possible accuracy under FCRA 607 ( b ). 

The continued reporting of : Incorrect name variations Incorrect addresses Incorrect employer information Unauthorized hard inquiries constitutes negligent and/or willful noncompliance under FCRA 616 and 617. 

These violations have caused : Damage to my credit profile Unfair credit denials Higher interest rates Emotional distress Ongoing risk of identity misuse The credit reporting agencies are not permitted to report information that can not be verified with competent evidence. They are also prohibited from reinserting previously removed information without proper written notice under FCRA 611 ( a ) ( 5 ). 

At this point, I am demanding the following corrective action : Immediate removal of all unauthorized hard inquiries listed above Permanent blocking of any information resulting from identity theft pursuant to FCRA 605B Removal of all inaccurate personal identifiers not properly verified Written confirmation of the method of verification used Written confirmation that reinvestigation was conducted manually and not solely through automated systems Failure to comply after receiving an FTC Identity Theft Report constitutes willful noncompliance with federal law. 

If these violations are not corrected immediately, I will pursue further action including escalation to state regulators, additional federal complaints, and civil remedies available under FCRA for statutory, actual, and punitive damages. 

I am requesting the CFPB to intervene and require the credit reporting agencies to fully comply with federal law and remove all fraudulent and unverified information from my consumer reports immediately.

text:
This complaint is a continuation of CFPB Case # XXXX and concerns U.S. Banks failure to refund the full escrow balance on a now-closed mortgage account ( Account XXXX, property at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX. 
I. U.S. BANK ISSUED AN INCOMPLETE ESCROW REFUND On XX/XX/XXXX, U.S. Bank issued an escrow refund check ( Check # XXXX ) in the amount of {$2200.00}, payable to XXXX XXXX. This amount corresponds exactly to the real estate taxes paid from escrow in XXXX, as documented on the XXXX IRS Form 1098 for this account ( Box XXXX : Real Estate Taxes Paid {$2200.00} ). 
However, XXXX Banks own XXXX Annual Tax & Interest Statement for this account shows an escrow ending balance of {$2200.00} that remains unrefunded. This balance represents insurance premiums that were collected from the previously confirmed Successor in Interest and previous owner of the property, XXXX XXXX, through monthly escrow deposits throughout XXXX but were never disbursed by U.S. Bank. 
The XXXX escrow reconciliation on U.S. Banks own statement reads as follows : Beginning Balance : ( {$1200.00} ) Deposits : {$5900.00} Insurance Paid : {$120.00} Taxes Paid : {$2200.00} Additional Assessments Paid : {$0.00} Escrow Disbursement : {$100.00} Ending Balance : {$2200.00} II. THE MISSING FUNDS ARE IDENTIFIABLE AND DOCUMENTED A comparison of insurance disbursements across the three most recent tax years makes the shortfall unmistakable : XXXX : Insurance paid from escrow {$2000.00} XXXX : Insurance paid from escrow {$2200.00} XXXX : Insurance paid from escrow {$120.00} U.S. Bank collected escrow deposits throughout XXXX at a rate of {$440.00} per month a rate calculated to cover both taxes and insurance. The taxes were paid ( {$2200.00} ) and subsequently refunded via the XX/XX/XXXX check. The insurance premium was never disbursed ( only {$120.00} of an expected ~ $ XXXX was paid ), and the resulting escrow surplus of {$2200.00} was retained by U.S. Bank XXXX 
U.S. Bank has provided no accounting, no explanation, and no refund of this {$2200.00} balance. 
III. RESPA REQUIRES RETURN OF THE FULL ESCROW BALANCE Under the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act ( RESPA ), 12 CFR 1024.34 ( b ), when a mortgage loan is paid in full, the servicer is required to return any amounts remaining in the escrow account to the previously confirmed Successor in Interest and previous owner of the property, XXXX XXXX, within 20 business days of the loan being paid off.

The statute does not permit a servicer to return only a portion of the escrow balance. It does not permit a servicer to selectively refund taxes while retaining insurance reserves. The obligation is to return the entire remaining escrow balance every dollar held in escrow that has not been disbursed for its intended purpose.

U.S. Banks refund of {$2200.00} covered only the tax component. The remaining {$2200.00} in escrow documented on U.S. Banks own annual statement has been withh
eld in violation of 1024.34 ( b ).

IV. U.S. BANK HAS ALREADY ACKNOWLEDGED ESCROW OBLIGATIONS ON THIS ACCOUNT In its XX/XX/XXXX response to CFPB Case # XXXX, U.S. Bank made a business decision to issue an escrow refund check. The check issued, however, accounts for only approximately half of the escrow funds held at the time of loan payoff. U.S. Bank did not provide any written accounting explaining why {$2200.00} in escrow reserves was excluded from the refund, nor did it identify any outstanding disbursement obligation that would justify retention of those funds. 
To be clear : U.S. Banks own 2025 Annual Tax & Interest Statement documents the {$2200.00} ending balance. This is not a disputed figure. It is U.S. Banks own number, on U.S. Banks own statement, for an account U.S. Bank has confirmed is closed and paid off. 
V. THIS CONTINUES A DOCUMENTED PATTERN OF MISHANDLING This incomplete refund is the latest in a multi-year pattern of escrow and account mismanagement by U.S. Bank on this account, documented across two prior CFPB complaints and multiple U.S. Bank response letters. 
CFPB XXXX # XXXX ( filed XX/XX/XXXX ) : This initial complaint addressed U.S. Banks refusal to issue any escrow refund whatsoever following loan payoff. At that time, U.S. Banks position was that XXXX XXXX had not been established as Successor in Interest and therefore was not entitled to escrow funds despite U.S. Bank having issued a formal written XXXX confirmation on XX/XX/XXXX, and having addressed its own XX/XX/XXXX settlement letter to XXXX XXXX ( Deceased ) and Successor In Interest XXXX XXXX before accepting {$11000.00} in certified funds from XXXX XXXX in that capacity. 
CFPB Case # XXXX ( filed XX/XX/XXXX ) : This follow-up complaint identified specific federal regulatory violations including : ( a ) U.S. Banks lack of legal authority under Regulation X to unilaterally revoke a confirmed SII designation ; ( b ) violation of 12 CFR 1024.34 ( b ) requiring return of escrow funds within 20 business days of loan payoff ; ( c ) promissory estoppel based on five years of conduct consistent with confirmed SII status ; and ( d ) a demand for a full written accounting of all escrow funds held. 
U.S. Banks own admissions across its XX/XX/XXXX, XX/XX/XXXX, and XX/XX/XXXX response letters confirm the following errors : On XX/XX/XXXX, U.S. Bank issued a formal XXXX confirmation letter to XXXX XXXX that U.S. Bank now claims was sent in error On XX/XX/XXXX, a U.S. Bank representative mistakenly discussed payoff information with XXXX XXXX without proper verification because the representative did not realize a death certificate was on file On XX/XX/XXXX, U.S. Bank incorrectly confirmed XXXX XXXX XXXX status by phone during the exact period he was completing the {$11000.00} settlement based on XXXX Banks own settlement letter designating him as SII On XX/XX/XXXX, U.S. Bank issued a settlement letter explicitly addressed to XXXX XXXX ( Deceased ) and Successor In Interest XXXX XXXX, accepted {$11000.00} in certified wired funds on that basis, and only after receiving those funds claimed the XXXX designation was invalid On XX/XX/XXXX, a U.S. Bank representative assisted XXXX XXXX on the account despite acknowledging he was not yet verified as XXXX and not authorized on the account at that time In its XX/XX/XXXX response, U.S. Bank stated that an administrative error does not establish Successor in Interest status and reliance on an administrative error does not substitute for documentation while simultaneously making a business decision to issue an escrow refund check, effectively acknowledging the obligation while disputing the legal basis The escrow refund itself was only issued under regulatory pressure. U.S. Bank refused to return any escrow funds until compelled to respond to the second CFPB complaint. Even then, U.S. Bank issued only a partial refund of {$2200.00} covering the tax component while retaining {$2200.00} in insurance escrow reserves without explanation or accounting. 
This is now the third time XXXX XXXX has been forced to seek regulatory intervention to compel U.S. Bank to meet basic servicing obligations on this closed account. The pattern is consistent : U.S. Bank withholds funds it is legally obligated to return, provides no accounting, and releases funds only under regulatory pressure and even then, incompletely.

I am submitting this complaint against American Express regarding ACH transfers initiated in XX/XX/year> from a XXXX  account ending in XXXX ( owned by XXXX XXXX ) to an American Express High Yield Savings account ending in XXXX ( owned by XXXX XXXX XXXX ). 

American Express allowed the XXXX account to be linked and verified through micro-deposits. Based on that verification, the transfers were accepted. The transfers were authorized, made in good faith, and represented repayment of a legitimate obligation to XXXX XXXX XXXX. At the time, American Express did not disclose or enforce any requirement that the linked external account be under the same name as the American Express account holder. 

After the funds were received in the American Express account, the account holder, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( my friend ), attempted to access the funds. At that point, American Express restricted the account and blocked access. Only after imposing that restriction did American Express state that the transfers could not be validated under its internal requirements. 

There is no fraud or unauthorized activity involved. American Express accepted the transfers but did not properly complete or apply them, and has retained the funds instead of returning them to the originating XXXX account. 

If the transfers did not satisfy American Express requirements, the linked account or the transfers should have been rejected before acceptance of funds. Once American Express determined the transfers could not be validated, it should have promptly reversed or returned the funds rather than continue to hold them. 

As a result, the funds remain in limbo : they have not been made available through the American Express account and have not been returned to the originating XXXX account. American Express is retaining funds without completing or reversing the transaction and, in communications, has indicated that action by the originating bank is required for return, while not returning the funds itself. 

I request that this matter be reviewed and that communication with American Express be facilitated to reach a clear and lawful resolution. Specifically, American Express should return the funds to the originating XXXX account without delay or coordinate directly with XXXX to complete that return. 

This situation raises concerns under established banking and consumer protection standards. Under XXXX XXXX XXXX for XXXX transfers, when a receiving institution can not properly complete or validate a transfer, the expected remedy is to return the funds rather than retain them indefinitely. In addition, the continued retention of funds that were not properly credited may raise concerns under Section XXXX of the Dodd-Frank Act relating to unfair or unreasonable practices. To the extent this matter involves an electronic funds transfer, it may also implicate obligations under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( Regulation E ) regarding proper handling and resolution. 

For these reasons, I request that this complaint be reviewed and that American Express resolve the matter by returning the funds or by taking immediate steps with XXXX to do so.

On XX/XX/XXXX, my leased vehicle ( XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ) was declared a total loss by my insurance company, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, Kia Finance America issued a Letter of Guarantee to XXXX  specifying a payoff amount of {$36000.00}. The letter explicitly stated that upon receipt of this amount, Kia Finance America agreed to " release and transfer all of its right, title and interest in and to the vehicle. '' Kia Finance included the original vehicle title with this letter, surrendering its possessory interest. Notably, nowhere in the Letter of Guarantee did Kia Finance reference " actual cash value, '' nor did it state that the payoff amount was subject to adjustment, revision, or reconciliation against any other figure. The amount was presented as final and unconditional. 

XXXX remitted payment in accordance with the amount Kia Finance requested. The title was transferred. I also made an additional payment of {$510.00} after the date of total loss, which Kia Finance applied to the account. 

Despite having authored the Letter of Guarantee, set the payoff amount, accepted payment of that amount, and surrendered the title, Kia Finance is now demanding an additional {$480.00}, claiming the " actual cash value '' of the lease obligation was higher than what they stated in their own Letter of Guarantee. This is the first time the concept of " actual cash value '' has been introduced into this transaction. If Kia Finance intended the payoff to be based on the actual cash value, it was their responsibility to state that amount or at minimum reference that methodology in the Letter of Guarantee. They did neither. They stated a specific dollar figure with no qualifications, caveats, or conditions, and all parties acted on that figure in good faith. 

Kia Finance not the insured and not the insurance carrier bore sole responsibility for calculating and stating the correct payoff figure. They are a sophisticated institutional lender with full access to account records, residual values, and every contractual term governing the disposition of the vehicle upon total loss. If the payoff amount should have been higher, it was their obligation to state that figure in the Letter of Guarantee. They did not. All parties relied on the figure Kia Finance provided. 

I have contacted Kia Finance multiple times to dispute this balance and have escalated repeatedly. They continue to demand payment of {$480.00} despite being unable to explain why their own Letter of Guarantee stated a different amount, and despite being unable to justify why the concept of " actual cash value '' was never mentioned in the Letter of Guarantee if that was the intended basis for the payoff. 

This conduct is consistent with the pattern the CFPB identified in its XX/XX/XXXX Supervisory Highlights for Auto Finance, where examiners found that servicers " sent deficiency notices to consumers and reported balances to third-party debt buyers that included inaccurate amounts in the deficiency balances owed by consumers. '' I am requesting that the CFPB investigate this matter and that Kia Finance be required to honor the payoff amount stated in its own Letter of Guarantee, confirm a {$0.00} balance, and refrain from reporting any derogatory information to consumer reporting agencies.

Section 623 imposes the following duties : Accuracy Guidelines The banking and credit union regulators and the CFPB will promulgate guidelines and regulations dealing with the accuracy of information provided to CRAs by furnishers. The regulations and guidelines issued by the CFPB will be available at consumer nance.gov/learnmore when they are issued. Section 623 ( e ).

General Prohibition on Reporting Inaccurate Information The FCRA prohibits information furnishers from providing information to a CRA that they know or have reasonable cause to believe is inaccurate. However, the furnisher is not subject to this general prohibition if it clearly and conspicuously speci es an address to which consumers may write to notify the furnisher that certain information is inaccurate. Sections 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) and ( a ) ( 1 ) ( C ).

Duty to Correct and Update Information If at any time a person who regularly and in the ordinary course of business furnishes information to one or more CRAs determines that the information provided is not complete or accurate, the furnisher must promptly provide complete and accurate information to the CRA. In addition, the furnisher must notify all CRAs that received the information of any corrections, and must thereafter report only the complete and accurate information. Section 623 ( a ) ( 2 ).

Duties After Notice of Dispute from Consumer If a consumer noti es a furnisher, at an address speci ed by the furnisher for such notices, that speci c information is inaccurate, and the information is, in fact, inaccurate, the furnisher must thereafter report the correct information to CRAs. Section 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( B ).

If a consumer noti es a furnisher that the consumer disputes the completeness or accuracy of any information reported by the furnisher, the furnisher may not subsequently report that information to a CRA without providing notice of the dispute. Section 623 ( a ) ( 3 ).

The federal banking and credit union regulators and the CFPB will issue regulations that will identify when an information furnisher must investigate a dispute made directly to the furnisher by a consumer. Once these regulations are issued, furnishers must comply with them and complete an investigation within XXXX days ( or XXXX days, if the consumer later provides relevant additional information ) unless the dispute is frivolous or irrelevant or comes from a credit repair organization. The CFPB regulations will be available at consumer nance.gov. Section 623 ( a ) ( 8 ).

Duties After Notice of Dispute from Consumer Reporting Agency If a CRA noti es a furnisher that a consumer disputes the completeness or accuracy of information provided by the furnisher, the furnisher has a duty to follow certain procedures. The furnisher must : Conduct an investigation and review all relevant information provided by the CRA, including information given to the CRA by the consumer. Sections 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( A ) and ( b ) ( 1 ) ( B ).

Report the results to the CRA that referred the dispute, and, if the investigation establishes that the information was, in fact, incomplete or inaccurate, report the results to all CRAs to which the furnisher provided the information that compile and maintain les on a nationwide basis. Sections 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( C ) and ( b ) ( 1 ) ( D ).

Complete the above steps within 30 days from the date the CRA receives the dispute ( or 45 days, if the consumer later provides relevant additional information to the CRA ). Section 623 ( b ) ( 2 ).

Promptly modify or delete the information, or block its reporting. Section 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( E ). 
Duty to Report Voluntary Closing of Credit Accounts If a consumer voluntarily closes a credit account, any person who regularly and in the ordinary course of business furnishes information to one or more CRAs must report this fact when it provides information to CRAs for the time period in which the account was closed. Section 623 ( a ) ( 4 ).

Duty to Report Dates of Delinquencies If a furnisher reports information concerning a delinquent account placed for collection, charged to pro t or loss, or subject to any similar action, the furnisher must, within XXXX days after reporting the information, provide the CRA with the month and the year of the commencement of the delinquency that immediately preceded the action, so that the agency will know how long to keep the information in the consumer 's le. Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ).

Any person, such as a debt collector, that has acquired or is responsible for collecting delinquent accounts and that reports information to CRAs may comply with the requirements of Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ) ( until there is a consumer dispute ) by reporting the same delinquency date previously reported by the creditor. If the creditor did not report this date, they may comply with the FCRA by establishing reasonable procedures to obtain and report delinquency dates, or, if a delinquency date can not be reasonably obtained, by following reasonable procedures to ensure that the date reported precedes the date when the account was placed for collection, charged to pro t or loss, or subjected to any similar action. Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ).

Duties of Financial Institutions When Reporting Negative Information Financial institutions that furnish information to nationwide consumer reporting agencies, as de ned in Section 603 ( p ), must notify consumers in writing if they may furnish or have furnished negative information to a CRA. Section 623 ( a ) ( 7 ). The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has prescribed model disclosures, 12 CFR Part 1022, App. B.

Duties When Furnishing Medical Information A furnisher whose primary business is providing medical services, products, or devices ( and such furnisher 's agents or assignees ) is a medical information furnisher for the purposes of the FCRA and must notify all CRAs to which it reports of this fact. Section 623 ( a ) ( 9 ). This notice will enable CRAs to comply with their duties under Section 604 ( g ) when reporting medical information.

Duties when ID Theft Occurs All furnishers must have in place reasonable procedures to respond to noti cations from CRAs that information furnished is the result of identity theft, and to prevent refurnishing the information in the future. A furnisher may not furnish information that a consumer has identi ed as resulting from identity theft unless the furnisher subsequently knows or is informed by the consumer that the information is correct. Section 623 ( a ) ( 6 ). If a furnisher learns that it has furnished inaccurate information due to identity theft, it must notify each consumer reporting agency of the correct information and must thereafter report only complete and accurate information. Section 623 ( a ) ( 2 ). When any furnisher of information is noti ed pursuant to the procedures set forth in Section 605B that a debt has resulted from identity theft, the furnisher may not sell, transfer, or place for collection the debt except in certain limited circumstances. Section 615 ( f ).

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau website, consumer nance.gov/learnmore, has more information about the FCRA. text:
We are filing a complaint regarding approximately {$3000.00} in credit card interest charges accrued between XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX in our Wells Fargo checking account that we believe resulted from a materially misleading payment and disclosure system. 
This issue is not about whether terms exist in the card agreement. It is about how the banks systems are designed and how information is presented to customers in practice. Across the payment interface, statements, and ongoing account communication, the bank consistently fails to clearly and effectively disclose how to avoid interest charges. 
The payment interface prominently emphasizes the minimum payment, while failing to clearly and conspicuously communicate that paying less than the full statement balance will immediately trigger high-interest charges ( often exceeding 20 % APR ). This creates a misleading impression that making the displayed payment is sufficient to manage the account responsibly. 
At the same time, the bank does not provide clear or proactive disclosure of interest being charged. There is no prominent summary, alert, or notification indicating that interest is accruing or has been incurred. Instead, interest charges are effectively buried within monthly statements, requiring detailed, line-by-line review to identify. As a result, it took multiple billing cycles before we became aware that interest charges were accumulating. 
Critically, the only location where the full payment obligation is clearly statedthe monthly statementis not reasonably accessible in practice. As paperless customers, we do not receive printed statements. The digital statement is not delivered directly, but requires navigating through multiple steps to access. In practice, customers rely on the app interface, which highlights the minimum payment and due date, while the full statement balance is not presented with equal clarity. The key information required to avoid interest is therefore effectively obscured. 
Taken together, these design choices create a system where customers are steered toward incurring interest charges without clear, timely, and actionable disclosure. This is not an isolated incident, but a structural issue that benefits the bank financially while impairing the customers ability to make informed decisions. In our case, this resulted in approximately {$3000.00} in interest charges accruing before we were able to identify the issue. 
We had sufficient funds to pay the full balance at all times. This was not a matter of inability or refusal to pay, but a direct result of a misleading and non-transparent user experience. 
We are requesting that these interest charges be refunded and that the bank review its disclosure and interface practices to ensure customers are provided with clear, prominent, and actionable information about how to avoid interest charges.

Approximately XXXX to XXXX months after the lease ended, I discovered today that a late payment had been reported to the credit bureaus for an outstanding balance of approximately {$300.00}. The original charges reportedly totaled approximately {$1000.00} ( a disposition/restocking fee of roughly {$400.00} and XXXX tire wear-and-tear charges of roughly {$300.00} each ), which were partially offset by an overpayment credit on my lease account. I have received no physical bill, no digital notification through the Chase app, no email, and no electronic communication of any kind regarding this balance. Chase claims they sent physical mail to my address, but throughout the entire lease term, all of my account communications were handled electronically. I had no reason to expect or look for a physical bill from Chase, and I did not receive one.

Chase also attempted to contact me by phone, but the voicemails left were extremely generic, stating only that someone from Chase was calling about an " important sensitive matter '' with no description of what it was about. The calls came from numbers I did not recognize. Given the prevalence of phone scams impersonating banks, these voicemails were indistinguishable from fraudulent calls and I did not return them.

I believe this constitutes inadequate notice under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, which requires that information reported to credit bureaus be accurate and that furnishers of credit information follow reasonable procedures to ensure the accuracy and fairness of their reporting. I am filing this complaint against Ally regarding auto account XXXX for my XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX.

On XX/XX/XXXX, when I attempted to trade in the XXXX toward another vehicle, the dealership evaluating it told me the XXXX was worth approximately {$22000.00} and that the airbags had deployed, making it rebuilt from California. That immediately raised serious concerns that the vehicle had been financed at an amount that did not reflect its true market value, actual condition, title history, and XXXX status.

On XX/XX/XXXX, and again on XX/XX/XXXX, I sent secure messages to Ally regarding Copy of Contract and underwriting loan. Allys own secure-message system showed those messages in sent status, and I also uploaded attachments proving that Allys portal would not provide the contract and that the app reflected no documents available. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, I formally disputed the account in writing and demanded a written investigation, a case or incident number, and the records needed to verify the legal and factual basis of the account. I specifically requested the executed retail installment contract and addenda, the full payment history, transaction ledger, suspense history, fee history, account notes, underwriting records, valuation records, title and title-history records, and the support for Allys negative credit reporting. I also specifically requested that Ally stop reporting inaccurate derogatory information while the account was disputed and under review. I then sent a second written notice requesting confirmation of receipt, a dispute/case number, a technical support ticket for the document-portal failure, and review by underwriting or the proper escalation department.

Instead of providing a meaningful written investigation, Ally repeatedly responded through secure messages that, due to the nature of the request, I needed to speak by phone. That was not a real investigation and did not answer the issues I raised. My secure messages and attachments already contained the proof, the requested records, and the specific dispute issues. Ally still failed to provide the written records or written findings I requested. 

Despite repeated written notice, Ally continued negative billing and credit reporting and then escalated into repossession. On XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX XXXX issued a Notice of Seizure and Disposal of Personal Property identifying Ally Servicing LLC as lienholder, stating that personal property was recovered from the vehicle on XX/XX/XXXX, that pickup would be by appointment only, that a handling fee might be assessed, and that personal property, including the license plate, would be disposed of on XX/XX/XXXX if left unclaimed. On XX/XX/XXXX, Ally sent a Notice of Our Plan to Sell Property stating that the vehicle would be sold at private sale sometime after XX/XX/XXXX and claiming {$4100.00} in past-due payments, {$500.00} in late charges, {$440.00} in retaking expenses, and a total of {$5100.00}.

This complaint is based on both Florida and federal consumer protections. Under Fla. Stat. 520.07, I was entitled to an exact copy of the retail installment contract and a written payment statement. Under Fla. Stat. 679.210, I was entitled to a written accounting or corrected statement of account. Under Fla. Stat. 679.609, 679.610, and 679.625, Ally and its agents were required to act lawfully in repossessing and disposing of the vehicle. Under Fla. Stat. 493.6118 and 493.6404, the recovery company was required to comply with law-enforcement notification, inventory, personal-property, and disposal requirements. Under Fla. Stat. 320.0609, my plate remains in my name. Under Fla. Stat. 559.72, Ally could not continue collecting and asserting rights in a misleading way while ignoring a reasonably disputed account. Under Fla. Stat. 319.14 and 501.204, the vehicles title history, rebuilt history, value, and disclosures remain central consumer-protection issues. In addition, under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2, and Regulation V, 12 C.F.R. 1022.43, Ally had a duty to reasonably investigate my direct dispute and correct inaccurate, incomplete, or unverifiable reporting.

text:
My complaint is in regards to the way Navient handles cosigner release. Their system is highly unfair and places unrealistic expectations onto borrowers, only to potentially be rejected anyway because application decisions are made at Navient 's discretion ( which I am certain means they have every right to reject any application simply because they feel like it and not for a legitimate reason ).

I applied for cosigner release once in the past, only to be told that I was ineligible for it due to my enrollment in an income-based repayment program ( which Navient itself does not offer ). I believed at the time this was due to my federal loans being enrolled in Income-Based Repayment ( IBR ) prior to my federal loans being serviced by XXXX. 

However, upon taking a closer look at the terms and conditions of cosigner release, I am also ineligible for this service currently because of the fact I am enrolled in an Extended repayment plan rather than the XXXX repayment plan. On top of this, I would also be expected to make twelve consecutive on-time payments, which is the only reasonable stipulation they have.

This is very unfair to borrowers. They and their cosigners should not be punished with ineligibility for cosigner release just because of the plan the borrower is enrolled in. Navient places too many obstacles in the way because they want to ensure that their borrowers never have the opportunity to release their cosigners. I can not speak for anyone else, but my cosigner is in their XXXX and they should not have to worry about having this hanging over their heads. 

In addition, it is my understanding that cosigner release, once the application is received, can take up to two years to go through and for the cosigner to actually be released from the borrower 's account. This is a wholly arbitrary and unnecessary period of time with no basis whatsoever in logic. There is no reason at all that simply removing a name from an account should take 24 months on top of everything else.

Furthermore, Navient requires a copy of the borrower 's credit report, college diploma, transcript. Again, more unnecessary documentation. It should not matter what my credit score is or whether or not I graduated college. Neither of these has any bearing at all on the debt someone holds with Navient.

I fully believe this is yet another attempt by Navient to discourage borrowers from trying to free their cosigners. This decision-making process should take no more than 6-8 weeks maximum. I have never once heard of anyone successfully having their cosigner released, either from Navient or any other student loan lender, so why is it even offered when no one can make use of it?

It also seems highly unnecessary for Navient to need to know things such as my employer, my income, my rent and my other monthly payments, as well as requiring proof of income and tax forms. Their only concern should be whether or not I make my payments to them every month. They have no need for this additional information, yet they require borrowers to fill out a form including all of this before they will even consider releasing the borrower 's cosigner.
label: Student loan

XXXX and Bridgecrest are controlled by XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX founder ) and his son XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX XXXX ), and operate an integrated dealer-captive lender structure that the CFPB has previously identified as presenting significant risk of consumer harm. 

I am filing this complaint to : ( 1 ) report a specific transaction exhibiting the same pattern the CFPB previously enforced against, and ( 2 ) request CFPB investigation into whether this pattern constitutes an ongoing unfair, deceptive, or abusive act or practice under the Consumer Financial Protection Act, 12 U.S.C. 5531.

DETAILS OF THE TRANSACTION : On XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX sold me a used XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  ( VIN : XXXX, XXXX miles ) for {$95000.00} a 20 % premium above the vehicle 's original new MSRP of approximately {$79000.00}. XXXX charged more for a XXXX-year-old used vehicle than the same vehicle cost when it was brand new. 

The purchase was financed at XXXX  % APR through Bridgecrest, XXXXXXXX XXXX affiliated captive lender. The Amount Financed was {$95000.00} over XXXX  months, producing approximately {$31000.00} in finance charges on the inflated principal. 

I have made XXXX consecutive on-time payments via AutoPay totaling {$76000.00} ( {$9000.00} down payment plus {$67000.00} in monthly payments ). I still owe {$50000.00} on a vehicle currently worth {$30000.00} {$33000.00}. I have been approximately {$18000.00} {$21000.00} underwater throughout the life of this loan despite a perfect payment history. 

THE PATTERN THE CFPB SHOULD INVESTIGATE : The CFPB 's own Data Spotlight on Negative Equity found that only XXXX  % of auto loans industry-wide are originated with negative equity. Independent analysis of XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX XXXX, XX/XX/XXXX ) found that approximately one-third of XXXX loans were underwater at origination XXXX to 4 times the industry rate. XXXX XXXX ( XX/XX/XXXX ) found that approximately 44 % of vehicles financed through XXXX since XXXX are underwater. The CFPB 's own data further shows that consumers who finance negative equity are more than twice as likely to face repossession within XXXX years. 

This is not an isolated incident. It is the predictable output of a business model that : 1. Prices vehicles above fair market value ( in my case, above the original new MSRP ) ; 2. Originates the financing through an affiliated captive lender that profits from interest on the inflated principal ; 3. Eliminates the independent lender underwriting check that normally protects consumers in arm's-length transactions ; 4. Bundles add-on products such as XXXX coverage into the financed principal, where they accrue interest at the loan rate ( in my case, {$1000.00} in XXXX coverage that accrues to approximately {$1500.00} with interest and which, by its own terms, does not cover the negative equity situation the transaction structure guaranteed at origination ). 

THE CORPORATE FAMILY 'S ENFORCEMENT HISTORY : In XXXX, the CFPB brought an {$8.00} XXXX enforcement action against XXXX for deceptive auto lending practices. XXXX is the parent entity controlled by XXXX XXXX XXXX. His son, XXXX XXXX XXXX, founded and serves as XXXX  of XXXX. Bridgecrest was established as the captive financing arm for both XXXX and XXXX. The structure the CFPB previously sanctioned has been replicated and scaled through XXXX. 

In XXXX, the CFPB sued XXXX XXXX XXXX, which operates the same integrated dealer-lender model, alleging that the company " misrepresented costs in loan agreements and tricked customers into high-cost loans on used cars '' by incentivizing dealers to inflate vehicle prices to increase loan principal balances. The parallels to XXXXBridgecrest 's operations are direct. 

CURRENT REGULATORY AND MARKET CONTEXT : XXXX is currently the subject of significant independent scrutiny : the XXXX XXXX XXXX report ( XX/XX/XXXX ) raised concerns about XXXX 's lending and accounting practices, and the XXXX XXXX report ( XX/XX/XXXX ) documented alleged accounting irregularities and {$800.00} XXXX in loan sales to a suspected undisclosed related party. The XXXX XXXX law firm has initiated a mass arbitration campaign against XXXX on behalf of consumers alleging similar unfair lending practices. 

PRE-ARBITRATION CONDUCT : On XX/XX/XXXX, I served a formal Claim Notice under Section XXXX of XXXX 's Arbitration Agreement. XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX team acknowledged receipt in writing and responded : " we are unable to modify or restructure financing terms. '' XXXX refused to engage in good-faith resolution of my claim. On XX/XX/XXXX, I filed a Demand for Arbitration with the XXXX XXXX XXXX under Case No. XXXX. 

VIOLATIONS ALLEGED : 1. Unfair, Deceptive, and Abusive Acts or Practices under CFPA, 12 U.S.C. 5531, by structuring a transaction that eliminates independent market discipline and systematically originates negative-equity loans at XXXX times the industry rate.

2. Deceptive pricing practices by offering a " discount '' relative to current new-vehicle MSRP while concealing that the price exceeded the vehicle 's own original new MSRP.

3. Deceptive sale of GAP coverage financed into the loan principal, where the coverage by its own terms can not address the negative-equity situation that the transaction was structured to create. 

DESIRED RESOLUTION : 1. CFPB investigation of XXXXBridgecrest lending practices, including the systemic origination of negative-equity loans at rates substantially exceeding industry norms ; 2. Principal reduction of my loan balance to align with the vehicle 's current fair market value ; 3. Reduction of the XXXX  % APR to a competitive rate ; 4. Disgorgement of the interest collected on the inflated portion of the principal ; 5. Such other relief as the CFPB deems appropriate. 

I have attached ( or will provide upon request ) : the AAA Demand for Arbitration, Supplemental Evidentiary Brief, Retail Installment Contract, and XXXX XXXX Resolution correspondence documenting XXXX 's refusal to engage in pre-arbitration resolution.

Dear CFPB : I am reaching out to you as a party who feels harassed by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and their attorneys at Forster and Garbus. We received a stipulation discontinuing action requesting that the case be dismissed with prejudice. 

These actions have affected me deeply. I am a former debt collector employed by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and I am well aware of the laws and compliance issues tied to the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ). I have felt harassed to such an extent XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX for the extreme amounts of duress these matters have placed on me. As a result of these actions and the undue stress they have placed on me, I am also now on short-term XXXX leave. The compounded stress of a loss in wages and the psychological torment of having started on the wrong foot at what should have been my dream job as a XXXX  XXXX at XXXX have created a situation that has led me to reach out to you in order to continue the work that I understand the CFPB had already begun. 

Of note, I find it troubling and feel harassed that after a consent order entered into in XXXX of XXXX that, among other provisions, contained an injunction from filing further unsubstantiated lawsuits until completion of an audit XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and Forster and Garbus still managed to file suit against my dear retired mother and I in XXXX and XXXX of XXXX. I remember vividly hearing the distress in the voices of consumers who at one point maintained that they paid some other debt collector for a debt that XXXX XXXX had recently started to collect on. text: For the past six months, Wells Fargo has willfully misinterpreted federal law to illegally threaten the acceleration of my mortgage loan. They are demanding that I formally " assume '' the loan as a condition to avoid acceleration, which is a direct violation of the Garn-St Germain Depository Institutions Act of 1982.1. Willful Misinterpretation of " Borrower '' ( 12 CFR 190.2 ( b ) ) Wells Fargo 's refusal to rectify this error stems from a narrowed definition of " Borrower '' that they claim only applies to the original signer of the note. However, federal regulations under 12 CFR 190.2 ( b ) which implements the Garn-St Germain Actexplicitly state : '' Borrower means a person who is a mortgagor, trustor, or other obligor of a real property loan, or any successor or assignee of such person. '' As the confirmed Successor in Interest to the late XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, I legally " step into the shoes '' of the borrower for the purposes of these protections.2. Violation of Protected Transfer Safe HarborsUnder 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3 ( d ) ( 8 ), a lender is prohibited from exercising a due-on-sale option for a transfer into an inter-vivos trust in which the borrower is and remains a beneficiary.XXXX  XXXX ( the Successor/Borrower at the time ) transferred the property to the trust while remaining the primary beneficiary.Upon his passing, I became the Successor in Interest.Because I am a named beneficiary in the trust, the " borrower '' ( myself, by federal definition ) remains a beneficiary.This transfer is federally protected and preempts any conflicting contract language or bank " approval '' requirements.3. Failure to Comply with Regulation XWells Fargo is also in violation of 12 CFR 1024.30 ( d ). The Official Interpretations ( Comment 30 ( d ) -1 ) clarify that a confirmed successor in interest must be considered a borrower for the purposes of mortgage servicing protections, regardless of whether they formally assume the loan obligation under state law. By continuing to demand an assumption under threat of foreclosure, Wells Fargo is engaging in unfair and deceptive servicing practices.Desired ResolutionI request that the CFPB compel Wells Fargo to : Cease all acceleration activities related to the transfer of the property to The XXXX XXXX Trust.Formally acknowledge my status as " Borrower '' pursuant to the definitions in 12 CFR 190.2 ( b ) and 12 CFR 1024.30 ( d ) .Withdraw the demand for loan assumption as a prerequisite for recognizing the federal safe harbor protections of the Garn-St Germain Act.Correct their internal records to show the loan is in good standing and not in violation of the mortgage contract.

I am writing to formally rebut MOHELAs most recent explanation regarding the approximately {$27000.00} increase in my federal student loan balance during the XXXX XXXX administrative forbearance period. 
After XXXX  months of continuous attempts to obtain a clear and accurate accounting, MOHELA has now provided an explanation that is not only unsupported by documentation but also inconsistent with the fundamental mechanics of federal student loan interest accrual and servicing practices. 
I. Core Issue This correspondence focuses exclusively on one issue : The unexplained addition of approximately {$27000.00} to my loan balance between XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX during a period in which my loans were subject to 0.0 % interest administrative forbearance under the XXXX XXXX. 
There were : No new loan disbursements, and No valid mechanism for interest accrual Under these conditions, the loan balance should have remained static, as it did during the XXXX administrative forbearance period. 

II. Summary of MOHELAs Explanation MOHELA now asserts that : Interest was incorrectly capitalized ( ~ {$25000.00} ) ; Their system calculates hypothetical interest and reduces it during 0 % periods ; Overlapping forbearance periods caused negative accrued interest ; This negative interest was later corrected, resulting in balance adjustments.

III. Technical Rebuttal This explanation is not credible for the following reasons : 1. Negative Interest Can not Exist in Federal Student Loan Accounting Under federal loan servicing rules : Interest may accrue ( positive ), or Be waived/subsidized ( effectively zero ) It can not become negative. 
If an internal system over-applies an interest reduction, the correct outcome is : Interest = {$0.00} not the creation of a borrower liability. 
There is no statutory or regulatory authority permitting a servicer to : Generate a negative interest condition, and Retroactively charge the borrower to correct it 2. 0.0 % Interest Means No AccrualNot Reversible Accrual MOHELAs claim that their system : calculates interest that would have accrued and reduces it is inconsistent with how 0 % interest is applied. 
Under a valid 0.0 % interest forbearance : Interest does not accrue at all It is not : o Accrued and then reversed o Simulated and adjusted This distinction is critical. Their explanation reflects a hypothetical accounting construct, not actual loan behavior.

3. Overlapping Forbearance Periods Can not Generate Debt Even if administrative overlaps occurred : The maximum impact would be over-suppression of interest to zero It can not : Produce a deficit Justify a retroactive charge Generate a {$27000.00} balance increase 4. Timing of the Alleged Correction Is Not Credible MOHELA claims this issue resulted in : A capitalization event on XX/XX/XXXX However : The relevant forbearance periods occurred in XXXX The adjustment occurred nearly XXXX XXXX  later This delay is inconsistent with legitimate servicing corrections and raises serious concerns regarding : Retroactive account reconstruction Post hoc justification of balance changes 5. Admission of Servicing Error Without Proper Remediation MOHELA explicitly states : interest was incorrectly capitalized This is an admission of a servicing error. 
However, instead of restoring the account to its correct pre-error state, MOHELA : Introduces an unverified negative interest correction mechanism Fails to reconcile the resulting balance This does not constitute remediationit represents replacement of one unsupported adjustment with another.

6. Absence of Required Supporting Documentation Despite repeated requests, MOHELA has failed to provide : A complete, itemized loan transaction history Daily interest accrual logs Any record showing a negative interest condition Calculation methodology supporting the {$27000.00} adjustment Audit logs or system-generated correction records Without this documentation, their explanation is non-verifiable and insufficient. 

IV. Formal Position Based on the above, MOHELAs explanation : Does not align with federal loan servicing principles Is unsupported by auditable financial records Fails to justify the {$27000.00} balance increase Accordingly, the balance adjustment remains formally disputed in full.

I am submitting this complaint regarding UMB XXXX XXXX refusal to make a one-time goodwill correction of a 30-day late payment that was reported to the credit bureaus on an otherwise long-standing, clean account.

text:
On XX/XX/2023 at XXXXXXXX XXXX I purchased a " Vanilla '' prepaid visa gift card at the XXXX XXXX located at this address : XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, CA XXXX I loaded {$190.00} onto the card. I paid a {$5.00} activation fee. The total cost of the card was {$200.00}. 

When I opened the packaging, I noticed several numbers on the front of the card and the expiration date had been scrapped off. This is despite the fact that the packaging was perfectly and completely sealed ( I'm aware of scams regarding these types of cards and am very careful about selecting a card off the rack. ) The next day I returned to the same XXXX XXXX  location with my receipt and asked for a refund. They informed me that they do not issue refunds for prepaid cards as part of their policy and that my only recourse was to work directly with the issuer of the card. 

I called the number on the back of the card and listened to the automated options. None of the options had anything to do with damaged cards. The only option that sounded like it would actually get me a person on the phone to talk with was the " lost or stolen card '' option, so I selected that. Within XXXX seconds I was on the phone with someone named " XXXX. '' I told XXXX the situation and he asked for the serial number on the back of the card. I gave it to him. He confirmed to me that {$190.00} was still loaded onto the card and that he would place a hold on the card. He asked me to take a picture of my driver 's license, my receipt ( front and back ), and the card itself ( front and back ) and email it to : XXXX with the subject line of the email being my case ID, which he provided me with. He said they would look at the information in my email and make a determination within 30 days and that if they judged in my favor I would be sent a replacement card in the mail. 

I did some digging online and found out that this has been an increasingly common occurrence in the past year. At first, I thought it was a scam involving someone coming into the store and meddling with the cards. But when realized that despite the front numbers being scratched off, the funds were loaded onto the card ( as confirmed via the serial number on the back -- which was not scratched ) it didn't make sense that some third party would go to the lengths to do this. And even if they wanted to, the classic scam usually involves taping or gluing another serial number over the original serial number so that the customer unwittingly loads someone else 's card. Such was not the case here. The packaging on my card was not tampered with. My funds were not stolen. They are still on the card. What happened here was a manufacturer defect in the production of the card. But it wasn't simply a case of low ink, there is some sort of white scuff mark ( extra material ) that is over the card itself where the numbers should be. 

I don't know for sure, but it sure would be a great scam if the company were doing this intentionally with a certain number of cards. Most people don't immediately open the cards. They purchase them for a friend or family member well in advance of a birthday or other special occasion. Then the recipient may not open the card for weeks or months. By the time the recipient opens the packaging and discovers the scuffs and lack of numbers, they have no recourse. They can call the number on the back of the card, but they're required to have the receipt. The problem is that the vast majority of consumers will not have the receipt. Even if they were to reach out to the person who bought them the card -- if it's been weeks or months the chances are slim to none that that person ( the original purchaser ) will have the receipt. Based on the number of complaints I've seen in the past year that exactly mirror my experience, it would not surprise me if hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars go unclaimed ( because many people won't even bother ) or unrestored ( because of those who do -- many will not have the receipt. ) It's very difficult to ascribe intent, but there is definitely a pattern here. And Incomm ( the parent company of Vanilla ) stands to gain millions of dollars due to these " errors. '' I count myself lucky that I held on to the receipt. Many are not so lucky. And most probably don't even bother doing anything once they're told they need a receipt. This has now taken about an hour and a half of my time and I'm more organized and assertive than most. What if it were a teenager who got this as a gift? Or an old person? Or someone who doesn't speak English? How would they have jumped through all the hoops I did? Especially without a receipt?
label: Prepaid card

TIMELINE On XX/XX/XXXX, PHH granted me a Temporary Hardship Forbearance Plan after I was forced to maintain dual housing due to an employer-directed relocation to XXXX, XXXX. I then submitted a complete Mortgage Assistance Application ( XXXX XXXX XXXX ) with all supporting documents. Advancing foreclosure proceedings while a loss mitigation application is pending constitutes prohibited dual-tracking under XXXX C.F.R. XXXX ( f ) and ( g ). 

On XX/XX/XXXX, at XXXX PM XXXX, I submitted a THIRD complete application via email to XXXX and XXXX, with copies to XXXX. The submission was XXXX MB and contained XXXX attachments : ( XXXX ) the completed and signed XXXX XXXX / Mortgage Assistance Application XXXX, signed by both borrowers on XX/XX/XXXX ; ( XXXX ) the completed and executed Hardship Affidavit / Letter of Explanation ; ( XXXX ) XXXX most recent bank statements dated within the last 90 days ; and ( XXXX ) XXXX most recent pay stubs from my employer, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX The subject line expressly stated " WITH PROOF OF PRIOR SUBMISSIONS. That auto-acknowledgment is a contemporaneous record that Onity received the complete package on XX/XX/XXXX. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, Onity Mortgage Corporation sent me a response letter that contains several admissions directly relevant to this complaint. Onity acknowledged receiving my XX/XX/XXXX " additional financial documents '' but wrote : " the application package was again determined to be incomplete. A denial letter confirming this determination will be issued.
